newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Mir officials treat commander, mull repair delay.
newsitem.headline: Mir officials treat commander, mull repair delay.

text.p: Doctors put the tired and stressed Russian commander of the crippled Mir space station on a course of drugs to combat a heart problem on Tuesday as ground staff scrambled to reschedule vital electrical repairs.

Russian and U.S. officials considered asking NASA physicist Michael Foale to step in during the risky operation for commander Vasily Tsibliyev, whom doctors said was under great strain and feeling a sense of responsibility after the accident on June 25 that has jeopardised the survival of the station.

Mission doctor Igor Goncharov told the 43-year-old Russian to start a course of sedatives and drugs to correct a slight irregularity in his heartbeat, first noticed on Sunday. The commander could be heard chuckling slightly and saying "Fine".

Mission Control on Tuesday cancelled the day's planned dress rehearsal of the electrical repair operation that would have involved Tsibliyev and flight engineer Alexander Lazutkin working intensively in clumsy spacesuits for six hours or more.

The rewiring in the now airless Spektr module, which was holed and sealed off after last month's collision, had been due to take place at the end of this week. Russian officials said it was now likely to be postponed for about a week -- giving Tsibliyev time to recover or Foale time to prepare for the job.

A NASA official at Mission Control in Korolyov outside Moscow said, however, that the Americans would need a day or two or even longer before being able to give the British-born Foale the go-ahead to stand in.
NASA would also question whether it might simply be better to put the job off until after a three-man Russian-French relief crew arrives on the Soyuz spacecraft on August 7.
"The decision has not yet been made and will probably not be made for at least 24-48 hours, possibly longer," NASA official Philip Engelauf said. "We're just going to take our time."

He told reporters NASA and the Russians would be looking at Foale's training records to help determine whether he had had the full relevant preparation for using a Russian spacesuit in the particular configuration needed during the planned repairs.
But he added: "We will also discuss with the Russians the urgency of this EVA (extra vehicular activity) against the potential of slipping it to some other Mir crew."

Mission control officials want to get the repair job over well before Soyuz blasts off from the Baikonur cosmodrome in Kazakhstan in case any extra equipment is found to be needed or, in the worst case, the 11-year old Mir has to be abandoned.
Goncharov sought to calm Tsibliyev during Tuesday's radio link up with Mir. "I repeat that we are assessing your work to be of the highest calibre," he said.

He also asked Tsibliyev to reduce his daily exercise routine. "We'll be monitoring you and monitoring how you feel...because the pulse and blood pressure are concerning us and we must control these parameters."

Asked what could have caused the problem, the doctor said it was most likely to be stress. "Naturally the inner anxiety, emotional stress and the feeling of responsibility which he is suffering is all having an effect on him," Goncharov said.

Russian media said officials blamed Tsibliyev for causing the June 25 accident -- the worst in the station's history -- by failing to reprogramme his controls to take account of waste being carried by the cargo craft he was manoeuvring.
Mission Control refused to confirm or deny the reports.

On a previous Mir flight, in 1993, Tsibliyev, a former Soviet air force pilot who has been on Mir this time since February, reportedly steered a remote vessel into a collision with the station, slightly damaging its exterior.
He and Lazutkin are due to return to Earth in late August.
